paras: The shooting of Canless Blair took place in or near Shelby, Cleveland County, North Carolina, in May 1882, when a sheriff's officer, B. F. Logan, wounded Blair, a Black man said to be an escaped convict, with rifle fire. A pistol shot that Blair was said to have fired at the officers struck George Wright, another Black man, in the leg. Blair survived and was jailed; the two papers that reported it told the officers' version.

According to the Charlotte Home and Democrat, Blair had been sent to the penitentiary and had escaped from its railroad guards a few weeks earlier. The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic said he had been sentenced for robbery several years before and had since robbed numerous houses.

In the Charlotte account, Blair was fleeing Sheriff Suttles and a posse in Shelby when he came near Deputy Sheriff Logan, drew a pistol and fired, hitting Wright, who was "standing by." Logan shot Blair in the shoulder blade, the two grappled and fell, and Wright clubbed Blair with a rifle. When Logan let go and Blair tried to run, two more rifle shots struck him in the thigh and right foot.

The Farmer and Mechanic's Hamlet correspondent called Logan the sheriff and said his posse met an unknown man on the road near Shelby who fired when spoken to. In that version one of the posse clubbed him, and Logan shot him three times in the legs as he ran.

Blair was placed in jail and, according to the Charlotte paper, confessed to several robberies in and around Shelby. Wright was described as not seriously hurt, a surgeon having extracted the ball from his leg.

Two white North Carolina papers carried the story: the Charlotte Home and Democrat on May 26 among brief items, and the Farmer and Mechanic on May 31 in its "Postal Card Notes from our Friends." Both told it from the officers' side: the Charlotte paper said Logan had been "violently assailed," and the Raleigh paper called Blair "a bad negro." Neither questioned the account of who fired first or the reported confession.
